summary: Sets out requirements for signaling protocols that work across different networks, administrative domains and technologies. Signaling here is mainly for quality of service, as with RSVP, but also covers uses such as MPLS label distribution and signaling to middleboxes. It is informational and came from the NSIS working group.

plainLanguage.summary: Signaling is like sending a note ahead asking the road to reserve space for you. This lists what a good note-passing system must be able to do.

subtitle: Framework for signaling protocols across network domains

tldr.problem: Quality of service and other network functions require signaling messages that cross administrative and technology domain boundaries, but there was no unified set of requirements for such signaling protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines comprehensive requirements for the NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling) framework, specifying how signaling should work across different network types and domains, including requirements for architecture, security, performance, and mobility.
tldr.outcome: These requirements enabled the development of NSIS protocols for QoS reservation, label distribution, middlebox signaling, and other network control functions that work across diverse network environments.

today: RFC 3726 remains the requirements document for the NSIS framework. While it is Informational and has not been obsoleted, actual NSIS implementations use companion protocols such as NSIS Transport Layer Protocol (NTLP) and General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST) to realize these requirements.

sections.title: Signaling Across Network Boundaries
sections.content:
RFC 3726 defines requirements for signaling protocols that work across different network environments, administrative domains, and technology types. Signaling is the mechanism by which applications and network nodes communicate to set up, modify, and tear down network services. While Quality of Service (QoS) and resource reservation are the primary examples, signaling is also used for label distribution in Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and for communication with middleboxes.

The challenge addressed by NSIS is that networks are heterogeneous: a single signaling flow may pass through access networks with different technologies, multiple administrative domains with different policies, and core networks with different capabilities. The requirements are designed to allow a unified signaling framework to work in all these scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Signaling is how applications ask the network for special treatment, like reserving bandwidth. The challenge is that the message has to work across different types of networks run by different companies.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Scope
sections.content:
The NSIS model defines three main entities. The NSIS Initiator (NI) starts the signaling process, usually triggered by an application or system in an end node. The NSIS Forwarder (NF) processes signaling messages along the signaling path, interacting with local resource management and propagating messages further. The NSIS Responder (NR) terminates the signaling and optionally interacts with applications.

The document distinguishes between path-coupled signaling, where messages follow the data path, and path-decoupled signaling, where signaling messages take independent paths. Path-coupled signaling must be supported; path-decoupled signaling is optional.

The scope includes the protocol to carry information and the semantics of that information, but excludes API design, transport layer adaptation mechanisms, provisioning algorithms, service definitions, and mobility decision-making.
sections.plainLanguage: Three entities are involved: one that starts the request, ones that pass it along and make it happen, and one at the end. The request can follow the data or take a different path.

sections.title: Architecture and Design Requirements
sections.content:
NSIS must be designed modularly to support both lightweight and full-featured implementations. The protocol must clearly separate the signaling protocol itself from the control information being transported, allowing the same information to be carried by different protocols in different scenarios.

The design must support independence of signaling from network control paradigms: the same NSIS protocol should work with different QoS technologies, different routing mechanisms, and different policy models. NSIS should also provide availability checking without requiring full state setup, enable carrying of opaque objects understood only by specific nodes, and work with any IP version without constraint.

Flexibility in placement is essential: NSIS Initiators and Responders can be located at end systems, network edges, or within the network. The architecture must support end-to-end signaling, end-to-edge, edge-to-edge, and network-to-network scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol should be simple enough to build cheaply but powerful enough to handle complex networks. It should work with different types of networks and let different companies put it in different places.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
Messaging requirements include the ability to explicitly erase state when no longer needed, automatic release of state after failures using soft-state timeout or explicit release mechanisms, and notification of state changes upstream. The protocol must notify the originator of both successful state establishment and refusal to establish state.

Control information must support mutability tracking so initiators can control which parameters can be modified by intermediate nodes. State must be addressable independently of flow identification, enabling state modifications during mobile handoffs. The protocol should support seamless modification of established state and optional grouping of multiple flow signals without transactional semantics.

Performance requirements include scalability to Internet scale for both core and access networks, low latency for rapid setup in mobile scenarios, low bandwidth consumption especially in wireless networks, ability to constrain device load, and high network utilization where needed. The protocol must work with flow aggregation at different levels and degrade gracefully under overload rather than failing catastrophically.
sections.plainLanguage: The signaling must handle errors, let different parts of the network add their own information, work with flows that move due to mobility, scale to huge networks, and not use too much bandwidth or computer power.

sections.title: Security, Mobility, and Interworking
sections.content:
Security requirements include strong authentication of signaling requests (not weak plain-text passwords), authorization mechanisms to prevent unauthorized state setup and service theft, integrity protection against modification, replay protection, hop-by-hop security for intermediate nodes that must process messages, and optional identity confidentiality and network topology hiding.

The protocol must provide denial-of-service protection through low computational complexity for verification before full authentication, and confidentiality of signaling messages on a hop-by-hop basis since intermediate nodes must read and potentially modify messages. State ownership must be protected with session identifiers to prevent adversaries from modifying established state.

For mobility, NSIS must allow efficient service re-establishment after handover, with re-establishment as quick as possible and localized where feasible rather than requiring end-to-end signaling. The protocol must interwork with IP tunneling (particularly IPSec), work with both IPv4 and IPv6, be independent from charging models, provide hooks for AAA protocols, work with seamless handoff protocols, and function with traditional L3 routing including route changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authorized users can make requests and nobody can fake one. The network must recover quickly when devices move to new locations, and work with different types of networks and security systems.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The requirements are tested against diverse scenarios including terminal mobility (devices moving between access points), wireless networks (3G, WLAN) with handover and spectrum management concerns, QoS signaling from access to core networks, inter-provider signaling across administrative boundaries, PSTN gateway integration requiring per-call admission control, and Virtual Private Networks with tunnel endpoints.

Each scenario presents unique challenges. Terminal mobility requires fast handoff with minimal packet loss. Wireless networks must handle low bandwidth, frequent handovers, and expensive leased lines. Access-to-core signaling typically involves aggregates with long lifetimes. Inter-provider signaling requires topology hiding and authorization checks. PSTN gateways require per-flow admission control at scale. VPNs introduce flow identification challenges when transport information is encrypted.

These scenarios demonstrate that a one-size-fits-all approach is insufficient; the protocol must support multiple operational modes and architectural patterns to succeed across the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Different networks have different problems: mobile devices that move, wireless with limited bandwidth, companies that need to work together, phone systems that need to set up calls, and private networks. The signaling must handle all of them.
